title: The Rotten Apple
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece tackles the difficult decision of removing a chronically negative or toxic team member, arguing that leaders routinely delay this call far longer than they should. It describes two archetypes of the 'rotten apple' and notes both are corrosive to team morale. The author walks through the common excuses leaders use to avoid termination and argues these rationalizations put the whole team at risk. Citing the centuries-old 'one bad apple spoils the barrel' proverb, the piece frames removal as nearly always the correct, if painful, decision.
points: Rotten apples come in two forms, chronic underperformers who blame others and toxic high performers who hoard credit, and both damage team morale.
Leaders commonly rationalize delay, but delay itself is what allows the damage to compound.
A leader's optimism about a person's potential to change can override the team's actual interest.
The centuries-old 'one bad apple' proverb is invoked to argue that removing a toxic team member is nearly always the correct call.
quotes: They are typically poor performers who blame everyone and everything for their weak performance. Their negativity and disrespect for others make them a nightmare for their peers.
In the rare case when the rotten apple is a high performer, they act as if everyone else owes their success to them. They hog credit and shift blame for anything that doesn’t go their way.
Avoiding or delaying the decision to terminate them places the team at risk.
The optimism leaders have in the potential of others to develop, improve, and perform can get in the way of an obvious decision. Good leaders don’t like giving up on anyone, even the rotten types.
The reality of “one bad apple spoils the whole barrel” applies to all teams. Removing the rotten apple from the team barrel as quickly as feasible is nearly always the best decision.
